title: Light-Cone Scaling of In-Circuit Noise in Randomized Measurements
authors: Pan Yu, Yan He, Yadong Wu
abstract: Randomized measurements provide an efficient way to extract physical properties of an unknown quantum state from limited data. On near-term hardware, gate and readout errors bias the reconstructed observables. Here we develop a microscopic description of this bias for locally scrambled shallow circuits. Independent local twirling reduces local implementation noise to stochastic Pauli damping, and a noise event contributes only when it overlaps the Heisenberg evolution of the measured Pauli operator. This gives an activated path-average formula for the noisy Pauli coefficient. In one-dimensional shallow circuits, the activated noise volume grows linearly with the size of a contiguous observable, leading to an exponential damping ratio. We verify this scaling for two-qubit random Clifford and locally scrambled iSWAP circuits with two-qubit Pauli noise, including spatial fluctuations and temporal drift. The scaling supports a small-string calibration protocol that predicts larger string observables without learning the full noisy measurement channel. Our result relates the noise bias of shallow-shadow protocols directly to operator-evolving dynamics.
summary: This paper develops a detailed theory describing how local noise corrupts measurements used to characterize unknown quantum states. It derives an exponential scaling law for this noise bias based on the geometry (light cone) of the measured observable. The result proposes a practical calibration protocol that allows researchers to estimate properties of large observables by only measuring small, easily accessible strings.
main_problem: The paper addresses how local gate and readout errors bias the reconstruction of quantum observables obtained via randomized measurements (like classical shadows) on near-term hardware.
main_result: It establishes an exponential scaling law for noise damping ($\log \eta_k \propto -k$) related to the 'light cone' geometry of the measured Pauli operator, enabling a small-string calibration protocol.
method: The authors develop a microscopic description using the Heisenberg picture and path averaging to derive an activated formula for the noisy Pauli coefficient, analyzed via cumulant expansion.
model_or_system: The analysis focuses on locally scrambled shallow circuits in one dimension, modeling noise as weak local CPTP channels independent of random gates. The system is studied using randomized measurements applied to quantum states.
key_observables: Damping ratio ($\eta_k$) quantifying the noise bias for an operator $\hat{P}_k$, and the scaling parameters $\alpha$ and $ eta$.
important_parameters: Circuit depth ($d$), size of contiguous observable string ($k$), and the nature/strength of local Pauli noise (e.g., anisotropic, fluctuating).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes weak local CPTP noise independent of sampled random gates; linear scaling is assumed to hold for large $k$ away from boundaries.
figures_summary: Figures demonstrate the exponential decay ($\log \eta = -\alpha k -  eta$) of the damping ratio for various circuits (Random Clifford, iSWAP) and show that small-string measurements can calibrate estimates for larger, complex observables.
paper_structure: The paper moves from developing a microscopic noise model based on activated path averaging to deriving the light-cone scaling law. It then verifies this scaling numerically using two-qubit circuits under various noise types, culminating in demonstrating a practical small-string calibration protocol.
why_interesting: This work provides crucial theoretical tools for quantifying and mitigating hardware imperfections (noise) in quantum characterization protocols, directly impacting the feasibility of running complex algorithms on NISQ devices by linking error to operator dynamics.
